questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presented following contact with a child with a maculopapular rash. She was 24 weeks pregnant. The exposure occurred 24 hours previously.
questions.lead_in: In pregnancy, human normal immunoglobulin is used as postexposure prophylaxis for what infection?
questions.explanation: Measles virus Postexposure prophylaxis with MMR vaccine is recommended for susceptible individuals exposed to proven cases of measles. Immunoglobulin is available for protection postexposure in those who are unable to have MMR, such as immunocompromised children or adults and pregnant women. Prophylactic regimens are not available postexposure to CMV , rubella, parvovirus B19, or HSV although specific testing and follow-up may be indicated.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q21

questions.stem: A 22 -year-old man presented with a 3-day history of subjective fever and sudden onset of behavioral changes and intermittent blurred vision. He also did not appear to fully recall the family members who brought him to the ED. He was never vaccinated against childhood diseases. He had no known exposures and did not endorse any insect bites, water, or animal exposures. The physical and neurologic exams were unremarkable. Investigations: CT brain: normal appearances A lumbar puncture was performed: CSF was clear with normal glucose and elevated protein of 85 mg/dL (reference range 15–60 mg/dL) CSF Gram stain: no organisms seen CSF multiplex panel negative CSF bacterial and viral cultures negative Two days after admission the patient developed a myoclonic jerk and his cognitive function continued to decline. An EEG showed period complexes occurring every 10 seconds. T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion-recovery (FLAIR) sequences from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed hyperintensity in the left frontal cortex. MRI performed 15 days later showed bilateral progression of the lesion. The patient continued to decline and died 60 days after admission.
questions.lead_in: What additional test result fits the diagnosis?

options.text: Bacterial culture positive for group A β-hemolytic streptococcus
IgM and IgG positive for West Nile virus in the serum and CSF
Increased measles IgG in the serum and CSF
Respiratory viral panel positive for parainfluenza virus

questions.explanation: Increased measles IgG in the serum and CSF The patient in this case has subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE). The patient was not vaccinated. Additionally, molecular testing as well as culture of the CSF for bacterial and viral pathogens is negative. The symptoms, imaging, and progression are consistent with SSPE. SSPE is a fatal complication resulting from persistent infection of the CNS with the measles virus. The typical presentation is 7–10 years after the initial measles infection, though this can vary. SSPE is typically seen in the pediatric population between 8 and 10 years old, though numerous cases with adult onset have been reported. SSPE typically progresses through four stages beginning with failure to learn at work and school coupled with personality changes and overall odd behavior. The second stage consists of myoclonic jerks, seizures, and dementia while the third stage progresses to unresponsiveness and rigidity. Finally, coma and autonomic failure make up the final stage. SSPE can progress rapidly with stages being indistinguishable or more slowly with a prolonged first stage. It affects males more often than females in the pediatric and adult populations. Ultimately SSPE results in the death of the patient. The diagnosis of SSPE is made by demonstrating elevated IgG to measles in the CSF and serum coupled with clinical signs and symptoms and a combination of other tests such as pathology, MRI and EEG which shows periodic complexes. SSPE is fatal in 95% of cases.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q3

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy developed fever, coryzal symptoms, and a dry cough. 48 hours later he developed a widespread maculopapular rash. He lived in rural Uganda. On examination his temperature was 39.5°C. He was noted to have bilateral conjunctivitis and white spots on his buccal mucosa.
questions.lead_in: What intervention has been shown to reduce mortality in such a child?
questions.explanation: Vitamin A supplements Most deaths attributable to measles occur in low-resource settings in children with poor access to healthcare and who have poor nutrition. Children with vitamin A deficiency appear to be at greater risk of severe measles resulting in increased mortality and morbidity. Vitamin A supplements have been shown to reduce overall mortality by up to 30% in children under the age of 5, with preexisting vitamin A deficiency and have been shown to have protective benefit in those complicated by pneumonia.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q26

questions.stem: A 25-year-old primigravida presents at 34/40 with a 1-day history of fevers, rash, dry cough, and coryzal symptoms. She had recently moved to the UK and was uncertain of her childhood vaccinations. On examination her temperature is 39°C, and there is a generalized maculopapular rash, which is coalescent on her trunk. Some small cervical lymph nodes are palpable bilaterally. There are small white spots on the buccal membrane beside her molars. She has bilateral conjunctivitis. She is concerned about the risk to her baby.
questions.lead_in: What are the possible adverse effects that she should be made aware of?

questions.model_answer:
a) Yes. Travel to a measles-endemic area is an indication for early MMR from 6 months of age; give one dose of MMR before departure.
b) The dose is not counted as valid: circulating maternal antibody neutralizes vaccine virus, so seroconversion rates and durability of immunity are lower. The infant must still receive the routine 2 valid doses on or after 12 months of age.

cohort_answer.text:

Doesn't confer long term immunity, maternal abs may inhibit seroconversion and therefore needs routine doses 12mos onwards

parts.text: What do you recommend as a means of measles prevention for her son?
Why do children less than 12 months respond less well to measles vaccine?

parts_raw.text: What do you recommend as a mean of measles prevention for her son?
b) Why do children < 12 months respond less well to measles vaccine?

questions.model_answer:
a) Give one dose of MMR before travel (early MMR is indicated from 6 months of age for travel to a measles-endemic country); this dose does not count toward the routine series.
b) Persistent transplacentally acquired maternal measles antibody neutralizes the live attenuated vaccine virus, and the infant immune system is relatively immature, so seroconversion rates are substantially lower.
c) Two valid doses on or after 12 months of age (routinely MMR at 12-15 months and a second dose at 18 months or by school entry).

cohort_answer.text: For children 6-12mo: give MMR vaccine (early), but this dose is not considered valid; 2 valid doses on/after 12mo required. Children<12mo respond less well: seroconversion rates much lower due to presence of maternal antibody. Doses after 12mo: 2 doses. Routine schedule: MMR given at 12-15mo, 2nd dose at 18mos - no later than school entry.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Fever (2) Cough (3) Coryza (4) Conjunctivitis (with Koplik spots pathognomonic and a maculopapular rash beginning on the face).
b) (1) Pneumonia (viral or bacterial superinfection) (2) Acute encephalitis (3) Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) (4) Otitis media/bacterial superinfection (death may result).
c) RT-PCR for measles RNA (or immunofluorescence for measles antigen). Two sample sites: (1) nasopharyngeal/nasal exudate secretions (2) urinary sediment (urine).
d) MMR (live measles) vaccine, given as post-exposure prophylaxis within 72 hours of exposure to prevent disease; she is immunocompetent and older than 12 months.
e) At 5 days she is outside the 72-hour vaccine window for reliable prevention; give immune globulin, which is effective if given within 6 days of exposure. MMR may still be offered to provide durable protection against future exposure.
questions.beyond_mandell: The specific 72-hour cutoff for post-exposure MMR and the 6-day cutoff for immune globulin are PHAC/CDC recommendations; Mandell states vaccine works if given shortly after exposure and IG must be given within 6 days.

cohort_answer.text:
Four classic symptoms: Conjunctivitis; Cough; Coryza; Maculopapular rash that begins on the face and spreads; Koplik spots; Fever
Four severe complications: Pneumonia; Acute encephalitis; Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (late complication); Myocarditis; Otitis media; Laryngotracheobronchitis; Diarrhoea
Test other than serology: RT-PCR. Sites: heparinized blood, nasopharyngeal aspirates, throat swabs, and urine
Post-exposure prophylaxis 48h (unvaccinated 2yo girl): MMR vaccine (ideally within 72 hours of exposure). Notes: Except in healthcare settings, unvaccinated people who receive their first dose of MMR vaccine within 72 hours after exposure may return to childcare, school, or work. Immunoglobulin (within 6 days of exposure): People who are at risk for severe illness and complications from measles, such as infants younger than 12 months of age, pregnant women without evidence of measles immunity, and people with severely compromised immune systems, should receive immunoglobulin. (MMR vaccine can be given instead if between 6 months and 12 months age). After receipt of IG, people cannot return to healthcare settings. In other settings, eg childcare, school, or work, factors such as immune status, intense or prolonged contact, and presence of populations at risk, should be taken into consideration before allowing people to return. Exclude healthcare personnel without evidence of immunity from duty from day 5 after first exposure to day 21 after last exposure, regardless of post-exposure vaccine.
Post-exposure prophylaxis 5 days (healthy non-pregnant woman working in daycare): If immunocompetent, susceptible – vaccinate to protect (PHAC recommendations is to vaccinate up to 6 days, but will also protect from future episodes). IVIG is for severely immunocompromised / pregnant woman or <6mos

questions.model_answer:
a) Airborne precautions (negative-pressure room, N95) plus standard precautions.
b) Assess the roommate's immunity; if susceptible give MMR within 72 hours (or immune globulin within 6 days if immunocompromised/contraindicated), and place the susceptible exposed roommate on airborne precautions from day 5 after first exposure to day 21 after last exposure.
c) Start precautions immediately on suspicion; remove 4 days after onset of rash in an immunocompetent patient (continue for the duration of illness if immunocompromised).
d) Contagious from several days before until several days after the onset of rash; virus has been recovered from respiratory secretions up to 48 hours after rash onset.
e) 3-year-old sibling: MMR vaccine (within 72 hours). 4-month-old sibling: immune globulin (infant younger than 12 months is at high risk and too young for routine vaccination).
questions.beyond_mandell: Airborne isolation timing (4 days after rash; day 5-21 for exposed susceptibles) is CDC/infection-control guidance; Mandell provides the infectious-period and IG-for-young-infant basis.

cohort_answer.text: Isolation precautions: Airborne + standard precautions. Roommate: Determine immunity or lack of; Vaccine within 72 hrs, if immunocompromised IVIG up to 6 days; if immune, no need to isolate. Start/remove precautions: Start immediately, can d/c 4 days after onset of rash, duration of illness for immunocompromised patients; if roommate was susceptible, airborne precautions from day 5 after 1st exposure to day 21 after last exposure. Period of infectiousness: 4 days before rash to 4 days after onset of rash. PEP for siblings: Vaccinate the 3 year old, Ig IM for 4 month old

questions.question: Measles: what is the mode of transmission, what is the late fatal neurologic complication, and what are two lab tests to confirm it?
questions.question_raw: Measles: What is the mode of transmission? What are late fatal neuro complication and two lab tests to confirm?

parts.text: Measles: What is the mode of transmission? What are late fatal neuro complication and two lab tests to confirm?

parts_raw.text: Measles: What is the mode of transmission? What are late fatal neuro complication and two lab tests to confirm?

questions.model_answer: Mode of transmission: airborne spread and direct contact with respiratory-secretion droplets (measles is among the most communicable infections, most infectious during the late prodrome). Late fatal neurologic complication: subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), occurring on average 7 years after measles, especially in children infected before age 2. Two confirmatory tests: (1) demonstration of unusually high measles antibody titers in both serum and CSF; (2) detection of measles RNA in brain tissue by RT-PCR (in situ RT-PCR has shown MV RNA in neurons and glia).

cohort_answer.text: Airborne Isolation. SSPE. Ratio of measles IgG in CSF to serum compared to the ratio of total albumin in CSF to serum (CSQrel). ADEM: acute disseminated encephalomyelitis. Measles inclusion body encephalitis. Electroencephalogram (EEG) during stage II may demonstrate bursts of high-voltage complexes (300 to 1500 microvolts) of two- to three-per-second delta waves (slow waves) and sharp waves. These complexes last 0.5 to 3 seconds and occur every 3 to 20 seconds. These EEG findings are characteristic of SSPE and may be pathognomonic. Computed tomography of the head may demonstrate atrophy and scarring. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain may be normal. PET may reveal substantial functional abnormalities. The serum anti-measles antibody concentration is elevated, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows elevated protein concentration and detectable anti-measles antibody. Post mortem diagnosis is definitive - brain tissue sent to path.

questions.model_answer:
a) Contagious from several days before until several days after the onset of rash; measles virus is recoverable from respiratory secretions only up to 48 h after rash onset (WHO operationally: ~4 days before to 4 days after rash).
b) No specific antiviral. Supportive care (antipyretics, hydration) plus vitamin A in two daily doses for 2 days for all children with acute measles; ribavirin is of unproven efficacy.
c) (1) Serum measles IgM by ELISA. (2) RT-PCR for measles RNA on nasopharyngeal/throat swab or urine.
questions.beyond_mandell: The '4 days before to 4 days after' operational window is WHO/CDC; Mandell states virus recoverable up to 48 h after rash and contagious 'several days' either side.

cohort_answer.text:
Period of infectivity: 1 day before start of prodrome until 48-96 hours after onset of rash (incubation 7-18 days from exposure) [Mandell: 48 hours; WHO: 4 days prior to rash to 4 days after rash erupts].
Treatment per WHO: No specific treatment. Symptom management (comfort, hydration to replace fluid loss from diarrhea/vomiting). All children and adults with measles should receive 2 doses of Vitamin A supplements 24 hours apart to prevent eye damage (xerophthalmia) and blindness (may also reduce measles deaths). Some suggest Ribavirin for patients <12 months (pneumonia) and >12 months with pneumonia requiring ventilatory support.
2 diagnostic tests: Clinical - cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots, maculopapular rash starting on the face. Serology - IgM+ (IgG for convalescent sera); IgM shows up 3 days after rash onset (undetectable by day 30), IgG positive day 7, peaks day 14. NAT/PCR - nasopharyngeal swab/throat swab, urine (10-20mL first void of day), heparinized blood. Viral culture - mononuclear cells, respiratory secretions, conjunctival swabs, or urine.

questions.model_answer: a) Measles: ssRNA, negative-sense (Paramyxoviridae); enveloped; no specific antiviral (vitamin A supportive; ribavirin only anecdotal in severe/immunocompromised disease). Mumps: ssRNA, negative-sense (Paramyxoviridae); enveloped; no specific antiviral - supportive care. Epstein-Barr virus: dsDNA (Herpesviridae); enveloped; no proven antiviral (herpesvirus DNA-polymerase inhibitors such as acyclovir/ganciclovir reduce shedding but not disease). Zika: ssRNA, positive-sense (Flaviviridae); enveloped; no specific antiviral - supportive care. Ebola: ssRNA, negative-sense (Filoviridae); enveloped; no small-molecule antiviral of proven benefit (remdesivir studied; licensed agents are monoclonal antibodies, i.e., immunotherapy). Influenza: segmented ssRNA, negative-sense (Orthomyxoviridae); enveloped; neuraminidase inhibitors - oseltamivir, zanamivir, peramivir (or baloxavir). Hepatitis B: partially double-stranded circular DNA (Hepadnaviridae); enveloped; nucleos(t)ide polymerase inhibitors - entecavir, tenofovir (or interferon-alfa). Coronavirus: ssRNA, positive-sense; enveloped with club-shaped spikes; remdesivir/nirmatrelvir-ritonavir for SARS-CoV-2.
questions.beyond_mandell: Baloxavir and SARS-CoV-2-specific agents (remdesivir, nirmatrelvir-ritonavir) postdate/lie outside this chapter; per IDSA influenza 2018 and IDSA COVID-19 guidance.

cohort_answer.text: Measles - Paramyxoviridae, ssRNA(-), enveloped: nothing (ribavirin trialed in severe cases, vitamin A). Mumps - Paramyxoviridae, ssRNA(-), enveloped: nothing. EBV - Herpesviridae, dsDNA, enveloped: nothing (GCV, cidofovir tried). Zika - Flaviviridae, ssRNA(+), enveloped: nothing. Ebola - Filovirus, ssRNA(-), enveloped: remdesivir, or Ervebo vaccine. Influenza - Orthomyxoviridae, ssRNA(-), enveloped: Oseltamivir/zanamivir/baloxavir. Hepatitis B - Hepadnaviridae, partially ds/partly ss circular DNA, enveloped: tenofovir, lamivudine, entecavir. Chikungunya - Togaviridae, ssRNA(+), enveloped: no Rx. Coronavirus - positive sense ssRNA, enveloped with club-shaped spikes.

Measles: RNA; enveloped; no specific antiviral (vitamin A adjunct; ribavirin unproven).
Hepatitis B: DNA; enveloped; yes - nucleos(t)ide analogues (tenofovir, entecavir), peginterferon.
